name: Anthony Edwards
notes: Georgia's SEC Freshman of the Year (19.1/5.2/2.8), a five-star, explosive rim-attacking scorer whose three-point range was considered a real limitation entering the league. Minnesota took him 1st. Edwards defied that exact concern — leading the NBA in made threes in 2024-25 (320, 7th-most in a season ever), a 4x All-Star and 2x All-NBA Second Team honoree, 2026 All-Star Game MVP, and 10,000 career points before turning 25 (joining LeBron and Durant), leading Minnesota to consecutive Western Conference Finals. Hit: a true franchise superstar who resolved the one weakness scouts flagged and became an elite two-way engine.

name: James Wiseman
notes: The consensus No. 1 recruit nationally, a Gatorade and Morgan Wootten National Player of the Year whose actual Memphis tenure was gutted to three games by an NCAA eligibility scandal involving Penny Hardaway — evaluators projected almost entirely off high school tape and a tiny college sample. Golden State took him 2nd. Wiseman flashed real ability immediately (19/6 debut) before a torn meniscus in 2021 started a chain of injuries; he collected a 2022 championship ring without playing a game, then bounced through Detroit, Indiana (an Achilles tear) and Toronto before multiple re-signings and releases. Bust: "widely regarded as an NBA draft bust" per his own Wikipedia summary — a top prospect whose evaluation was always incomplete, and whose NBA career was defined by injuries rather than production (9.0/5.5 career).

name: LaMelo Ball
notes: A player who skipped college for pro stints in Lithuania (a rough go) and then Australia's NBL, where he broke out (17/7.4/6.8, NBL Rookie of the Year) after scouts had marked him as a possible second-rounder — an extreme swing in evaluation inside one year. Charlotte took him 3rd. Ball delivered on the late-rising hype: Rookie of the Year, the youngest triple-double in NBA history, multiple All-Star selections, a $205.9M extension, and a 50-point game in 2024-25, though ankle injuries have repeatedly interrupted seasons, leading to a July 2026 trade to Minnesota. Hit: a wildly unconventional pre-draft path that produced a genuine, if injury-touched, NBA star.

name: Patrick Williams
notes: A Florida State freshman sixth man (9.2/4.0, ACC Sixth Man of the Year) ranked just 21st among 2020 prospects by ESPN — real athletic and defensive versatility upside taken at 4th overall on projection more than production. Chicago took him. Williams's rookie flash (9.2 ppg) never grew into more — 9-10 ppg with declining efficiency across subsequent seasons, a 2021 wrist surgery and later foot issues slowing development, regressing to 7.0 ppg by 2025-26. Bust: a developmental top-5 bet on a thin freshman sample that never paid off as a difference-maker.

name: Isaac Okoro
notes: Auburn's SEC All-Defensive freshman (12.9/4.4/2.0), elite perimeter defense with clear offensive limitations (29% from three) flagged as the swing factor for a small forward. Cleveland took him 5th. Okoro settled into a defense-first role player career (career 8.3/2.8 across five Cleveland seasons, All-Rookie Second Team) before a 2025 trade to Chicago (for Lonzo Ball) saw a modest scoring uptick (9.3 ppg). Mixed outcome: exactly the elite-defense, limited-offense wing scouted, never developing into more.

name: Onyeka Okongwu
notes: USC's First-Team All-Pac-12 freshman (16.2/8.6/2.7 blk, a school-record 8 blocks in his debut), elite rim protection and efficiency cut short by the COVID-canceled tournament. Atlanta took him 6th. Okongwu needed patient bench development (4.6 to 8.2 ppg over two seasons) before a real breakout — a $62M extension, then a genuine starter's role by 2025-26 (career-high 15.2 ppg on 37.6% from three). Solid outcome: the elite-defense freshman finally became a real two-way starting-caliber big, on a longer timeline than his draft slot implied.

name: Killian Hayes
notes: A French lead guard with off-the-charts pick-and-roll vision and elite live-dribble passing (albeit heavily left-handed), real shooting-development questions flagged as the swing skill. Detroit took him 7th. A rookie-year hip labral tear set back his start; Hayes's best season (10.3/6.2 in 2022-23) never repeated, and he was waived by Detroit in 2024, bouncing through Brooklyn, Cleveland and Sacramento without recapturing that form. Bust: the exact shooting-development question flagged pre-draft never resolved, capping a genuinely gifted passer's NBA ceiling.

name: Obi Toppin
notes: Dayton's consensus National Player of the Year as a redshirt sophomore (a school-record 190 dunks, 63.3% FG), spectacular athleticism with real questions about shooting range and all-around offensive skill beyond finishing. New York took him 8th. Toppin's Knicks role stayed limited (4.1 ppg as a rookie, a 2022 Dunk Contest title as his signature moment) before a 2023 trade to Indiana unlocked a real role — a $60M extension and a starting role in the Pacers' 2025 Finals run. Mixed outcome: a real, valuable NBA rotation big once given a fair opportunity, never quite the star his college dominance implied.

name: Deni Avdija
notes: An Israeli EuroLeague wing (Maccabi Tel Aviv) projected as a consensus top-5 talent who nonetheless slipped, real ball-handling and IQ versatility undercut by shaky free-throw (59%) and three-point (33%) shooting in Israel. Washington took him 9th. Avdija battled an ankle fracture before developing steadily (14.7/7.2 by 2023-24), then fully broke out after a 2024 trade to Portland — a 2025-26 season averaging 24.2/6.9/6.7 and the first Israeli-descent NBA All-Star. Hit: a top-5-caliber talent who slipped on draft night and eventually delivered exactly that star-level outcome.

name: Jalen Smith
notes: A five-star Maryland sophomore (15.5/10.5/2.4 blk, First-Team All-Big Ten and All-American), elite rebounding and shot-blocking production. Phoenix took him 10th. Smith's Phoenix run stayed marginal (2.0-6.0 ppg, a 2021 Finals appearance without much of a role) before a 2022 trade to Indiana finally unlocked real minutes (9.4-9.9 ppg), then a $27M Bulls deal in 2024 and continued solid production (9.2/6.1) before a season-ending calf injury in March 2026. Solid outcome: a real, sustained NBA rotation big once given a genuine opportunity, never quite the anchor his college dominance suggested.

name: Devin Vassell
notes: A Florida State sophomore who rose to first-round consideration on shooting (41.9%, then 41.5% from three across two seasons) and defensive versatility. San Antonio took him 11th. Vassell developed into the Spurs' scoring focal point (19.5 ppg by 2023-24), a franchise-record $146M extension, a 37-point game, and continued as a cornerstone (13.9 ppg) on San Antonio's 2026 playoff team. Solid outcome: a genuine, sustained franchise building block, just below true All-Star status.

name: Tyrese Haliburton
notes: Iowa State's three-star-turned-star, an elite passer (a program-record 17 assists, a 4.5 assist-to-turnover ratio) with an unconventional shooting motion that raised real consistency questions, his final college season cut short by a wrist fracture. Sacramento took him 12th. Haliburton became a genuine superstar after a trade to Indiana — back-to-back All-Star and All-NBA selections, an assists title, historic playoff clutch shooting, and a 2025 Finals run defined by multiple triple-doubles — before a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the Finals ended the run and cost him the entire 2025-26 season (Indiana went 19-63 without him). Hit: the unconventional shooting motion never stopped him from becoming a top-tier playmaking star, injury the only thing slowing him down.

name: Kira Lewis Jr.
notes: Alabama's teenage sophomore breakout (18.5/5.2/4.8 on 45.9/36.6% shooting, First-Team All-SEC), real scoring and playmaking upside from one of the draft's youngest players. New Orleans took him 13th. Lewis's rookie year (6.4 ppg) never grew before a torn ACL and MCL in December 2021 wiped out most of a season, and his role shrank across New Orleans, Toronto and Utah stints before a 2024 shift to the G League. Bust: real youthful upside that a devastating knee injury never let fully develop.

name: Aaron Nesmith
notes: Vanderbilt's abbreviated sophomore explosion (23.0/4.9 on a historic 52.2% from three across 14 games) cut short by a foot injury, elite shooting efficiency on a tiny, incomplete sample. Boston took him 14th. Nesmith developed gradually (real 2022 Finals minutes) before a 2022 trade to Indiana fully unlocked him — a near-50-40-90 season (2024-25), a $40.4M extension, and a starring role in Indiana's 2025 Finals run. Hit: the elite-shooting flashes from an injury-shortened college season became a genuine, sustained NBA starter.

name: Cole Anthony
notes: UNC's five-star, top-ranked point guard recruit who set an ACC freshman debut scoring record (34 points) before a torn meniscus slowed his season (18.5/5.7/4.0 overall), real shot-creation talent with an already-present durability flag. Orlando took him 15th. Anthony peaked in 2021-22 (16.3/5.7 across 65 starts) before his role steadily shrank, a 2025 Memphis trade and buyout, a brief Milwaukee stint, and by August 2026 a move to Australia's NBL. Bust: real point-guard talent that never sustained beyond one strong Orlando season.

name: Isaiah Stewart
notes: A five-star Washington freshman (17.0/8.8/2.1 blk, First-Team All-Pac-12) once considered top-3-caliber talent, elite physical tools with real skill-refinement questions typical of a one-and-done big. Portland took him 16th (traded through Houston to Detroit). Stewart developed into a real, physical Pistons frontcourt piece (All-Rookie Second Team, a $64M extension) over six seasons, his tenure complicated by disciplinary incidents (ejections, a 2024 arrest, a 2026 suspension for a brawl with Miles Bridges) before a 2026 trade to Memphis. Hit: real, sustained NBA frontcourt production, alongside real off-court volatility.

name: Aleksej Pokusevski
notes: A 7-foot, 18-year-old Olympiacos product who made his EuroLeague debut at 17, real long-term upside on thin, unrefined production (10.8/7.9/3.1 in Greece's second division). Minnesota took him 17th (traded to Oklahoma City). Pokuševski flashed real rotation minutes early (8.2, then 7.6 ppg over two seasons) before a leg injury and declining trust collapsed his role to 1.2 ppg by 2023-24, waived shortly after. Bust: real long-term physical upside that never developed into consistent NBA skill.

name: Josh Green
notes: A five-star Arizona freshman (12.0/4.6/2.6 on 36.1% from three), real athletic two-way versatility with ball-handling and decision-making the flagged growth areas. Dallas took him 18th. Green developed gradually (2.6 to 9.1 ppg over four seasons) into a real Mavericks rotation piece, including their 2024 Finals run, before a 2024 six-team trade to Charlotte (7.4 ppg, 68 starts) and, after shoulder surgery, further trades landing him in Utah by 2026. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-year NBA rotation wing, never quite the two-way star his recruiting profile implied.

name: Saddiq Bey
notes: Villanova's Julius Erving Award winner as the nation's top small forward (16.1/4.7 on 47.7/45.1% shooting, unanimous First-Team All-Big East), real size-shooting combination questioned mainly on athleticism. Brooklyn took him 19th (traded to Detroit). Bey delivered immediately — All-Rookie First Team, a 51-point game, a franchise three-point record — before a 2023 trade to Atlanta and a torn ACL in March 2024 derailed the momentum; a 2024 move to Washington and then New Orleans, with a 42-point comeback game in February 2026, suggests real recovery. Solid outcome: a genuine, productive NBA scoring wing at his peak, injury interrupting further growth.

name: Precious Achiuwa
notes: A five-star Memphis freshman and AAC Player and Freshman of the Year (15.8/10.8/1.9 blk), elite athleticism and rebounding with offensive skill and IQ the typical one-and-done question marks. Miami took him 20th. Achiuwa developed gradually through Toronto (a 9.2/6.0 peak) and New York (part of the OG Anunoby trade) before a 2025-26 Sacramento season produced a career-high 10.1 ppg across 73 games and a re-signing through 2027. Mixed outcome: a real, steadily-improving NBA rotation big across three teams, never quite a full-time starter.

name: Tyrese Maxey
notes: A top-15 Kentucky recruit whose freshman season (a 26-point debut record) ended prematurely with the COVID-canceled SEC/NCAA tournaments, real speed and scoring instincts on a thin sample. Philadelphia took him 21st. Maxey's chance came when Ben Simmons refused to play; he seized it — a 52-point game, the 2023-24 Most Improved Player award and first All-Star selection (the first player ever to win MIP, make an All-Star team and win the Sportsmanship Award in the same season), a $204M extension, and a 2025-26 All-Star start and All-NBA Third Team. Hit: a mid-first-round talent who became Philadelphia's franchise cornerstone.

name: Zeke Nnaji
notes: A five-star Arizona freshman (16.1/8.6 on 57% FG, Pac-12 Freshman of the Year and First-Team All-Pac-12), real efficient production questioned mainly on translatable NBA role. Denver took him 22nd. Nnaji never grew beyond marginal bench minutes (3.2 to 6.6 ppg, career sub-4 ppg) despite a $32M extension in 2023 and a 2023 championship ring earned in a reserve role. Bust: a dominant college freshman season that never produced a real NBA role, championship ring notwithstanding.

name: Leandro Bolmaro
notes: An Argentine wing (Nike Hoop Summit World Team) taken more on international projection than a detailed scouting record. New York took him 23rd (traded to Minnesota) on a $11.8M rookie deal. Bolmaro's NBA chance was brief and unproductive (49 total games, 27.0% shooting) before a 2023 shift to Europe — where he's become a genuine standout, the 2026 Lega Serie A Defensive Player of the Year with Olimpia Milano. Bust at the NBA level, a real European defensive star since.

name: R.J. Hampton
notes: A top-6 recruit who skipped college for New Zealand's NBL under the Next Stars program, real athletic upside on modest per-game production (8.8/3.9/2.4) that dropped him from projected top-5 to 24th. Denver took him. Hampton flashed real rookie-of-the-month-caliber promise after a trade to Orlando (16 points in his first start) but never sustained it (7.6-11.2 ppg range), bouncing through Detroit and Miami two-way deals before a shift to China. Bust: real athletic tools from an unconventional path that never became consistent NBA production.

name: Immanuel Quickley
notes: Kentucky's SEC Player of the Year as a sophomore (16.1/4.2), a real shooting-guard prospect whose exact recruiting rank varied widely between services. Oklahoma City took him 25th (traded to New York). Quickley developed into a genuine scoring guard — a 40-point game, runner-up Sixth Man of the Year — before a trade to Toronto (part of the OG Anunoby deal) fully unlocked him as a lead ball-handler, earning a $175M extension and a January 2026 Player of the Week honor. Hit: a mid-first-round Kentucky guard who became a legitimate franchise-caliber starter.

name: Payton Pritchard
notes: Oregon's Bob Cousy Award winner and Pac-12 Player of the Year as a senior (20.5 ppg, the program's all-time assists leader), elite production tempered by athletic limitations typical of a smaller guard. Boston took him 26th. Pritchard developed patiently through a 2022 Finals run into a genuine weapon — the 2025 Sixth Man of the Year (an NBA reserve three-point record), a 2024 championship, and a 2025-26 move into the starting lineup with career-high across-the-board numbers (17.0/3.9/5.2). Solid outcome: a late-blooming college star who became a real, award-winning NBA contributor.

name: Udoka Azubuike
notes: Kansas's NABC Defensive Player of the Year and a record-setting finisher (74.9% career field goal percentage, mostly dunks, a 7'7" wingspan), elite interior efficiency completely dependent on the rim given zero perimeter game. Utah took him 27th. A 2022 foot surgery derailed his development, and Azubuike never exceeded marginal minutes (3.0/2.8 across three Jazz seasons) before a modest Phoenix stint. Bust: exactly the one-dimensional offensive limitation flagged pre-draft, compounded by injury, kept him off NBA rotations.

name: Jaden McDaniels
notes: A consensus top-10, potential-No.-1-caliber Washington freshman (13.0/5.8, an 18-point debut) whose move to the bench during conference play hinted at defensive-consistency concerns. LA Lakers took him 28th (traded through Oklahoma City to Minnesota). McDaniels developed into a genuine two-way star — a $136M extension, All-Defensive Second Team, career-high 30-point and 32-point playoff games, and 82 consecutive games played in 2025-26 (14.8 ppg). Hit: a former potential-No.-1 talent who slipped to 28 and became a real All-Defensive-caliber starter.

name: Malachi Flynn
notes: San Diego State's Mountain West Player and Defensive Player of the Year (17.6/5.1/4.5, a 36-point game, the first Aztec first-rounder since Kawhi Leonard), real two-way combo-guard skill. Toronto took him 29th. Flynn's rookie flashes (7.5 ppg) steadily declined (4.3, then 4.6 ppg) despite one bizarre 50-point bench outburst with Detroit in 2024, and he bounced to the G League, a brief Charlotte 10-day deal, and Turkey by 2025. Bust: real college two-way production that a lack of NBA opportunity never let show up consistently.

name: Desmond Bane
notes: A completely unranked recruit (no D-I offer until his senior year of high school) who broke out as a TCU senior — Big 12-leading 44.2% three-point shooting, First-Team All-Big 12 — pure shot-making from total obscurity. Boston took him 30th (traded to Memphis). Bane became one of the great late-first-round value outcomes: All-Rookie Second Team, a 23.7 ppg peak season, a $207M max extension, and after a 2025 trade to Orlando a full 82-game starting season averaging 20.1 ppg. Hit: an unrecruited high schooler who became a genuine All-Star-caliber NBA scorer.

name: Tyrell Terry
notes: A Stanford freshman sharpshooter (14.7/4.5/3.2 on 40.8% from three, 89.1% FT) who reportedly broke an NBA front-office basketball-IQ testing record, elite processing and shooting on a slight frame. Dallas took him 31st. Terry barely played (11 games, 5.1 minutes) before a brief Memphis hardship stint and a 2022 waiver, and after a short comeback attempt in France, he retired from professional basketball at 22, citing anxiety and mental health reasons. Bust: elite testing metrics and shooting that a lack of opportunity, and ultimately his own well-being, never let translate to the floor.

name: Vernon Carey Jr.
notes: A five-star, sixth-ranked Duke recruit and National Freshman of the Year (17.8/8.8/1.6 blk, First-Team All-ACC), dominant interior size and production. Charlotte took him 32nd. Carey never found NBA minutes (37 total games across Charlotte and Washington, 1.9/1.4) despite the elite college pedigree, his career shifting to the G League and Turkey before returning to the G League by the mid-2020s. Bust: a National Freshman of the Year whose college dominance never once translated to an NBA role.

name: Daniel Oturu
notes: Minnesota's Second-Team All-Big Ten sophomore breakout (20.1/11.3/2.5 blk, a 30-point upset of Michigan), real rim protection and rebounding with limited perimeter range (37% from three) and NBA-level athleticism the flag. LA Clippers took him 33rd. Oturu never secured real NBA minutes (33 total games, 1.9 ppg across the Clippers and Toronto) before his career shifted to Turkey and Israel, where he's posted real double-digit scoring. Bust at the NBA level, a legitimate scorer overseas.

name: Théo Maledon
notes: A French EuroLeague point guard (ASVEL) considered the favorite for EuroLeague Rising Star, real advanced playmaking and a developing shot (36%+ from three) clouded by a pre-draft shoulder injury and modest scoring questions. Philadelphia took him 34th (traded to Oklahoma City). Maledon's rookie year (10.1 ppg, real rotation minutes) proved to be the ceiling — production collapsed through Charlotte and Phoenix stints (down to 17 combined games by 2023-24) before a 2025 return to Real Madrid. Bust: a promising rookie season that never repeated, the career ultimately reverting to Europe.

name: Xavier Tillman Sr.
notes: Michigan State's Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year (13.7/10.4, famous for guarding Zion Williamson in an Elite Eight upset), a conditioning-focused, defense-first four/five with a clearly limited scoring role. Sacramento took him 35th (traded to Memphis). Tillman developed into a real, useful Grizzlies rotation big (207 games, 6.1/4.2) before a 2024 trade to Boston brought him a genuine championship ring, though his role shrank afterward, leading to a 2026 trade to Charlotte and a move to Turkey's Trabzonspor. Solid outcome: a real, multi-year NBA rotation role and a championship, exactly the defense-first four/five scouted.

name: Tyler Bey
notes: Colorado's Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Year and Most Improved Player across his final two seasons (13.6-13.8/9.0-9.9), real two-way production and rebounding. Philadelphia took him 36th (traded to Dallas). Bey's NBA chance was brief and unproductive (18 games, 1.0 ppg) before his career shifted overseas — a genuine standout since, the 2023 Israeli League scoring leader, plus stops in the Philippines, Lebanon and Venezuela. Bust at the NBA level, a real international scorer since.

name: Vít Krejčí
notes: A 19-year-old Czech guard developing with Basket Zaragoza in Spain's ACB (modest per-game numbers, ACB All-Young Players Team), a pure long-term projection pick. Washington took him 37th (traded to Oklahoma City). Krejčí rehabbed an ACL tear before debuting, then developed patiently through Atlanta — a two-way deal, a $10M extension in 2024, real per-game growth to 9.0 ppg by 2025-26 — before a 2026 trade to Portland. Mixed outcome: a real, slowly-earned NBA rotation role from a thin developmental starting point.

name: Saben Lee
notes: Vanderbilt's second-Team All-SEC junior breakout (18.6/3.5/4.2/1.5 stl), real scoring and ball-handling from an undersized (6'2") lead guard. Utah took him 38th (traded to Detroit). Lee spent his early career mostly on two-way deals (Detroit, then Philadelphia and Phoenix G League stints, a 25-point/10-rebound double-double flash) before never securing a permanent NBA role, his career shifting fully to Europe by 2024 — Turkey, Israel's Maccabi Tel Aviv, a 2025 Greek league title with Olympiacos, and Lithuania's Žalgiris by 2026. Bust at the NBA level, a genuine, well-traveled European winner since.

name: Elijah Hughes
notes: Syracuse's First-Team All-ACC junior scorer (19.0/4.9/3.4 on 34.2% from three career), real volume scoring from a proven college system. New Orleans took him 39th (traded to Utah). Hughes never found consistent NBA minutes (54 games across Utah and Portland, 2.9 ppg on 32.8% shooting) before his career shifted to Spain and Germany. Bust: elite college scoring volume that never crossed over to NBA-level shot-making efficiency.

name: Robert Woodard II
notes: A four-star Mississippi State recruit (his state's highest-rated prospect) who broke out as a sophomore starter (11.4/6.5), real two-way tools from a rapidly-improving college season. Memphis took him 40th (traded to Sacramento). Woodard never secured real NBA minutes (25 games across two Sacramento seasons, 1.1/1.1) despite the recruiting pedigree, his career shifting to the G League and then France and Greece by 2023. Bust: a rapidly-improving college sophomore season that never got a real NBA chance to build on.

name: Tre Jones
notes: A five-star Duke recruit and ACC Player and Defensive Player of the Year as a sophomore (16.2/6.4/1.8 stl), elite point-of-attack defense and vision with a modest jumper (31% from three) the flag. San Antonio took him 41st. Jones developed patiently into the Spurs' primary point guard (12.9/6.6 as a 65-game starter), re-signed for $19M, then traded to Chicago in 2025 and signed a $24M deal, averaging 14.1 ppg in his most recent season. Solid outcome: a real, sustained starting-caliber NBA point guard built on exactly the defense-and-vision skill set scouted.

name: Nick Richards
notes: A Jamaica-discovered five-star Kentucky recruit who broke out as a junior (14.0/7.8/2.1 blk, First-Team All-SEC), real rim protection and improving offensive polish. New Orleans took him 42nd (traded to Charlotte). Richards needed two quiet development years before a real breakout (9.7/8.0 by 2023-24, a $15M extension) and a strong Phoenix debut (21/11) after a 2025 trade, before further moves to Chicago and a 2026 Miami signing. Mixed outcome: a real, sustained NBA starting-center stretch, though a well-traveled one.

name: Jahmi'us Ramsey
notes: Texas Tech's program-record five-star recruit, a Big 12 Freshman of the Year (15.0 ppg on 42.2/42.6% shooting), elite one-and-done scoring efficiency. Sacramento took him 43rd. Ramsey never secured real NBA minutes (3.1-3.2 ppg across two Sacramento seasons, heavy G League time, a brief Toronto 10-day stint) before his career shifted to Italy. Bust: a program-record recruit whose shooting efficiency never got a real NBA opportunity to show up.

name: Marko Simonovic
notes: A Montenegrin big man (Mega Basket) taken 44th by Chicago as a draft-and-stash-style project pick, with limited detailed pre-draft scouting record available. Simonovic's NBA chance with the Bulls never developed into consistent production, and his career has continued largely in Europe (Olimpija Ljubljana among his stops). Bust: a projection pick whose NBA opportunity never turned into a real rotation role.

name: Jordan Nwora
notes: Louisville's First-Team All-ACC junior and runner-up Player of the Year (18.0/7.7 on 44% FG), real scoring and rebounding versatility with playmaking (1.3 assists) and perimeter defense the flags. Milwaukee took him 45th. Nwora won a championship ring as a rookie in a reserve role, developed modest Bucks production (5.7-7.9 ppg) before a 2023 trade to Indiana produced real scoring flashes (a 33-point game, a franchise second-quarter record), then a 2024 trade to Toronto and a shift to Turkey's Anadolu Efes and, by 2025, Serbia's Crvena zvezda. Mixed outcome: a real NBA role and championship ring, career ultimately continuing in Europe.

name: CJ Elleby
notes: Washington State's First-Team All-Pac-12 sophomore breakout (18.4/7.8, preseason Julius Erving and Wooden watchlists), real go-to scoring production. Portland took him 46th. Elleby never developed beyond marginal Trail Blazers minutes (4.6 ppg across 88 games over two seasons) before his career shifted to the G League and international stops in Israel, Mexico and Turkey. Bust: a real college scoring breakout that never crossed over to consistent NBA opportunity.

name: Yam Madar
notes: An Israeli guard (Hapoel Tel Aviv) who turned pro at 17 and won the Israeli League's youngest-ever Most Improved Player award, a genuine developmental prospect. Boston took him 47th. Madar never signed an NBA contract — a lone Summer League look was the extent of it — instead building a real EuroLeague career: a 2023 Rising Star honor with Partizan, a Turkish League title with Fenerbahçe, and by 2026 a return to Maccabi Tel Aviv. Never played in the NBA — a genuine, still-developing EuroLeague talent instead.

name: Nico Mannion
notes: A five-star Arizona freshman and top point guard recruit (14.0/5.3, All-Pac-12 Second Team), real playmaking pedigree from a thin one-season sample. Golden State took him 48th. Mannion's NBA chance was brief and unproductive (30 games, 4.1/1.5/2.3 in 2020-21) before his career shifted fully to Europe — a 2022 EuroCup title with Virtus Bologna and a 2024 Italian league scoring title with Varese. Bust at the NBA level, a genuine Italian league star since.

name: Isaiah Joe
notes: Arkansas's record-setting freshman shooter (an SEC freshman record 113 threes at 41.4%) who broke out further as a sophomore (16.9/4.1) before a knee procedure, elite shooting volume on a slight (165 lb) frame the flag. Philadelphia took him 49th. Joe's Sixers stint stayed marginal (3.6-3.7 ppg) before a trade to Oklahoma City fully unlocked him — a $48M extension, career-high scoring outbursts (33, then 31 points), and a 2025 championship (41.1% from three across 21 playoff games) — before a 2026 trade to Detroit. Solid outcome: elite shooting that, given a real opportunity, became a genuine championship-caliber NBA role.

name: Skylar Mays
notes: LSU's First Team All-SEC senior and Academic All-American of the Year (16.7/5.0), a smart, winning floor general without elite measurables. Atlanta took him 50th. Mays needed two-way seasoning before a standard NBA contract in 2022, and his career became a well-traveled journey across the G League, Mexico, Portland, the Lakers, Turkey's Fenerbahçe, and by 2026 Australia's South East Melbourne Phoenix. Mixed outcome: a real NBA contract eventually earned, never more than fringe roster depth.
